newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's fiscal policy shift seen within limits.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's fiscal policy shift seen within limits.

text.p: Mexico's slightly looser fiscal policy signals a shift away from supporting monetary policy, but economists said they do not see the 1997 budget deficit getting out of hand.
Economists said that Mexico is gradually loosening its fiscal stance, after lending a helping hand over the last two years to reducing the current account deficit and controlling inflation.

Last week the federal government said its budget deficit for 1996 was 0.09 percent of gross domestic product, in part due to a 20 billion peso settlement with the government's bank support program, Fobaproa.
As Mexico's Banorte noted in a report, 1996 was the first year in four years to register a budget deficit.
While the government has forecasted a budget deficit of 0.5 percent of GDP in 1997, many economists have said it could be larger.
Mexico's Bancomer forecasted a deficit of 0.8 percent, while other forecasts placed it as high as 2.0 percent of GDP.
J.P. Morgan forecasted a deficit of 1.0 percent of GDP in 1997, Alfredo Thorne, the company's chief economist in Mexico, said.
"The fiscal policy is shifting in the opposite direction and is trying to be the main instrument for sustainable growth, and that is why we see it on the loose side," Thorne said.
"The 1.0 percent is not a big concern but it does signal that fiscal policy is no longer helping monetary policy to control inflation," he said.
Economists noted that the government kept the nation's finances under control during the worst of the crisis in 1995, and see the government continuing to be able to manage any small budget deficits.

"They (the federal government) have established their credibility as fiscally sound. During the period when things were the most serious they were able to keep the fiscal side sound," said HSBC James Capel economist Gray Newman.
With important mid-term elections set to take place in Mexico in July, some observers have worried that the government might try to loosen monetary or fiscal policy to sway voters.
The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI)'s control of Congress is at stake as are the governorships of six states and the mayorship of Mexico City.
But with the central bank publishing daily monetary base targets, and a close watch on public sector spending, concerns about on-balance-sheet spending getting out of control have been downplayed.

"I do not think that there will be pressure on the public finances that will create a larger deficit due to expenditures for, as some people have claimed, buying votes," said Bancomer economist Carlos Rosales.
Government expenditures rose sharply in the fourth quarter, when the deficit increased to 3.1 percent of gross domestic product in the same quarter, economists said.

That knocked down the primary surplus to 0.4 percent of GDP in the fourth quarter from 4.6 percent of GDP in the third quarter. The fiscal expansion was covered by the surplus from the first three quarters.
Government expenditures are seen rising in the first half of 1997, as the government aims to invest more in private sector infrastructure projects, analysts said.
